sentence: The NHS says prostate cancer may not cause any symptoms at first.
When symptoms do appear, they are mainly changes to passing urine.
The NHS lists needing to pass urine more often, getting up in the night to pass urine, difficulty starting or keeping a steady stream, and a weak flow.
Blood in the urine is also listed.
Later symptoms can include lower back pain, tiredness and weight loss without trying, which the NHS links with more advanced disease.
Many of these symptoms have other causes, such as an enlarged prostate, and having them does not mean a person definitely has prostate cancer.
note: NHS: enlarged prostate is another cause of raised PSA; symptoms not definite.

sentence: Because early prostate cancer may cause nothing noticeable, the absence of symptoms does not rule it out.

sentence: Macmillan describes age as the strongest risk factor, with prostate cancer uncommon under the age of 50 and more common over 75.
The NHS lists being over 50, being from a Black ethnic background and having a family history of prostate cancer as factors that raise risk.
Macmillan adds that Black men are also more likely to develop prostate cancer at a younger age, and that the reason is not clear but may involve genetic factors.
Macmillan says having a father or brother with prostate cancer raises a man's risk, and that the risk is greater if the relative was diagnosed under 65.
BRCA2 gene variants have the clearest link among inherited gene changes, according to Macmillan.
The NHS also notes that close relatives with pancreatic, breast or ovarian cancer, particularly at a young age, can be a sign that inherited genes are involved.
The NHS says there is no national screening programme for prostate cancer.
A PSA blood test is not routinely offered on the NHS, with the exception of people whose genetic tests have shown a faulty BRCA2 gene.
The NHS says a man can still ask a GP for a PSA blood test even without symptoms, and the GP will consider his cancer risk to help decide whether the test is right for him.
A PSA blood test measures a protein made by the prostate. The NHS says a high result does not mean a person has cancer, because other causes such as an enlarged prostate are possible.
note: NHS PSA page; PSA definition is textbook-level.

sentence: If a specialist suspects cancer, the next step is an MRI scan.
If more information is needed, a biopsy may be suggested, in which a small needle is put into the prostate to take a tissue sample to be checked for cancer cells.
If cancer is confirmed, further tests such as a CT scan, MRI scan, PET scan or bone scan may be used to help plan treatment.
The NHS says prostate cancer often grows slowly and may never cause problems, so monitoring is a common first step for some people.
Active surveillance involves regular PSA tests, MRI scans and sometimes biopsies, so that any sign of progression is found as early as possible.
NHS 111 Wales says it aims to avoid unnecessary treatment of harmless cancers while still treating men who need it.
When treatment is needed, the main options are surgery to remove the prostate, radiotherapy and hormone therapy, and chemotherapy may be needed if the cancer has spread.
Hormone therapy reduces the effect of testosterone on the cancer, and the NHS says it does not cure prostate cancer on its own but can slow it down and help with symptoms.
Brachytherapy is a form of radiotherapy delivered from inside the prostate.
Treatments have side effects. Surgery and radiotherapy can both affect urine control and erections.
Radiotherapy can also cause tiredness, diarrhoea and bowel irritation, and hormone therapy can cause hot flushes, tiredness, weight gain, reduced sexual desire and thinning of the bones.
The NHS 111 Wales page notes that prostate cancer can come back after treatment, and that a doctor can estimate the chance of this from factors such as the PSA level and the stage of the cancer.

A clinical summary of the ProtecT trial reports that deaths specifically from prostate cancer were low at a median of 10 years whatever treatment men were assigned, and that active surveillance is reasonable for some men.
